---
title: "Audit Monitoring, Security, and Sharing"
---


::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Distinguish continuous auditing from continuous monitoring, and exceptions from anomalies, and specify a monitoring test by its rule, population, frequency, and expected result.
2. Build an exception register in Power Query that turns the flags of several tests into one table of exceptions, with a table of tests and the populations needed for rates.
3. Build a monitoring page that shows exception counts and rates by test and month and lets a reviewer drill through to the documents behind them.
4. Define row-level security with a dynamic role and a maintained security table, and test it with View as.
5. Audit an access design: where its mapping comes from, which tables its rules reach, who bypasses it, and which pages it leaves silently partial.
6. Recommend how a report should be published and shared, considering licenses, workspace roles, apps, refresh, public links, and sensitivity labels.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

It is May 2027, and you are back on the internal audit team of Chapters 8 and 12. The chief audit executive brings three requests. The first comes from the audit committee. The tests of Chapters 8 and 12 found journal entries approved by the people who created them, purchase orders approved after the approver had left the company, and pay approved by the employee being paid. The committee wants to know every month whether such exceptions recur, rather than wait for the next annual review. The second comes from the controller, who is about to give each department manager access to Charles River Reports, the package of Chapters 13 to 15, so that each can follow their own cost center against its budget. Before it goes out, internal audit must review who will see what. The third comes from management, which wants a recommendation on how the package should be published and shared.

Your task is to build a monitoring report for internal audit, to review and test the security of the controller's package, and to set out how both should be shared. This chapter teaches continuous monitoring and the design of an exception register, a monitoring page that leads from exception counts to documents, row-level security and how to audit it, and the ways a Power BI report reaches its readers.


## From Audit Tests to Monitoring

Chapter 8 tested whole populations once, in a workbook, and Chapter 12 saved its tests as a library of queries that the team could run again every quarter. Monitoring takes the next step: the same tests run every period, on new data, with the results kept and compared over time. Vasarhelyi and Halper (1991) described one of the first such systems, built for the internal auditors of AT&T Bell Laboratories, which measured key figures of large systems, compared them with standards, and called the auditors' attention to problems as they arose. Two decades later, continuous auditing had moved from research into practice in many firms (Alles et al., 2008).

Two terms describe this work, and they differ in who does it. Continuous auditing is internal audit's use of technology to assess risks and controls on an ongoing basis, so that it can give the board and management assurance throughout the year rather than once (Institute of Internal Auditors [IIA], 2025). Continuous monitoring is management's own ongoing review of whether its controls operate as designed. Many auditors hold that monitoring belongs to management, not to internal audit, but effective continuous auditing depends on strong monitoring, and internal audit can help a business build it (Tronto & Killingsworth, 2021). In this chapter you build a monitoring report as internal audit's tool, and the same tests could be handed to management to run as its own monitoring.

Monitoring tests are of two kinds. Kogan et al. (2014) separate a first layer that checks deterministic business rules, such as an approval within the approver's limit, from a second layer of analytical monitoring that looks for unusual patterns. A rule either holds or fails, and a failure is an exception in the sense of Chapter 8, a record that meets a test's criteria and therefore needs an explanation. An analytical test produces anomalies: records or periods that differ from what is expected, such as two payments of the same amount to the same supplier a few days apart, or first digits that depart from Benford's Law. An anomaly is a reason to look, not yet a failure. The exception register you build in this chapter holds the rule tests; the anomaly tests of Chapters 8 and 12 return in the exercises.

A monitoring system that runs every month can produce more exceptions than anyone can review. Alles et al. (2006) found that preventing such alarm floods was one of the critical tasks in implementing continuous monitoring at Siemens, and Li et al. (2016) proposed ranking exceptions by how likely each is to be an error or fraud, so that reviewers start with the most suspicious. A practical first defense is design: each test should state its rule, its population, how often it runs, and what result is expected, as each query of Chapter 12's audit query library did, so that a reviewer can tell an expected exception from a new one. Metcash, an Australian distributor, ran more than a hundred automated tests daily, with an integrated system for managing their exceptions and visual reports for reviewing them (Hardy & Laslett, 2015). @tbl-16-01 lists the tests of this chapter, all of them rules that Chapters 8 and 12 have already run once, each with the process whose documents it tests.

| TestID | Test | Process | Chapter |
|------------|------------------------------|--------------|------|
| JE Weekend | Entry created on a weekend | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE Backdated | Entry created after its posting date | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE SelfApproved | Entry approved by its creator | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE AboveLimit | Entry above its approver's limit | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE RoundAmount | Entry in whole thousands | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| PO SelfApproved | Order approved by its creator | Purchase orders | Chapter 12 |
| PO AboveLimit | Order above its approver's limit | Purchase orders | Chapter 12 |
| PO AfterTermination | Order approved after the approver left | Purchase orders | Chapter 12 |
| PR PaidBeforeApproval | Pay made before the register was approved | Payroll | Chapter 12 |
| PR AfterTermination | Pay period ending after termination | Payroll | Chapter 12 |
| PR SelfApproved | Register approved by its own employee | Payroll | Chapter 12 |

: The monitoring tests {#tbl-16-01}

Who sees the results matters too. Gonzalez and Hoffman (2018) found in an experiment that telling people promptly which of their transactions a monitoring system had flagged also told them what it could not detect, and that when the system was weak, prompt notification made participants more inclined to commit fraud. A monitoring report is therefore internal audit's working paper. It goes to the people who oversee the controls, not to the people whose approvals it tests, which is why this chapter builds it in a file of its own rather than as pages of the controller's package. @fig-16-01 shows the cycle a monitoring test follows.

![The Monitoring Cycle.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-01-monitoring-cycle.svg){#fig-16-01 fig-alt="A cycle diagram. A rule runs on each period's population and produces exceptions; the exceptions go to internal audit's monitoring report, where each receives a disposition; dispositions feed back into the rule, its threshold, or the control. A side panel distinguishes continuous auditing, run by internal audit for assurance, from continuous monitoring, run by management on its own controls, and notes that the exceptions go to the people who oversee the controls, not to those whose transactions are tested."}


## Designing an Exception Register

An exception register is a single table that holds the exceptions of every monitoring test, one row for each exception of each test, with the same columns whatever the test: the test that found it, the document, its date, its amount, and the employee responsible, here the approver. Chapter 12 built the same thing in SQL, when UNION ALL stacked the exceptions of several queries into one result, each labeled with the test that found it. In Power BI the register is built in Power Query, so that every refresh runs the tests again on the new data. @tbl-16-02 shows where each column comes from in the three processes this chapter monitors.

| Register column | Journal entries | Purchase orders | Payroll registers |
|------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| TestID | JE and the flag name | PO and the flag name | PR and the flag name |
| DocumentNumber | EntryNumber | PONumber | Register and its ID |
| EventDate | PostingDate | OrderDate | PayDate |
| Amount | TotalAmount | OrderTotal | NetPay |
| EmployeeID | ApprovedByEmployeeID | ApprovedByEmployeeID | ApprovedByEmployeeID |

: The columns of the exception register {#tbl-16-02}

The register takes three moves. First, each test becomes a flag column, 1 if the record fails the rule and 0 if it passes, the Power Query counterpart of the flag formulas Chapter 8 wrote in the columns of an Excel table, and the flags of a document add up to its risk score. Second, unpivoting turns the flag columns of a table into rows. Each record becomes one row per flag, with the flag's name in a column named Attribute and its value in a column named Value (Microsoft, 2025h), and keeping only the rows whose value is 1 leaves exactly the exceptions. Third, appending stacks the exception tables of the three processes into one (Microsoft, 2026a). Append is Power Query's counterpart of UNION ALL, with one difference that matters: UNION ALL matches columns by their position, while Append matches them by their names, and a column that one table lacks is filled with nulls. Each exception table must therefore rename its columns to the register's names before the append, or the result has a DocumentNumber column that is empty for one process and a PONumber column that is empty for the others.

A count of exceptions means little without the size of the population it came from. A dozen exceptions among a few hundred journal entries and a dozen among many thousands of purchase orders are very different rates. The register therefore sits beside the populations it tests, which stay in the model as fact tables of their own, and a measure divides the exceptions of each test by the documents of its process. The populations are also what the auditor reconciles before relying on the tests, as Chapters 8 and 12 did: if the journal entries in the model do not add up to the journal entry postings in the ledger, the monitoring is testing an incomplete population. @fig-16-02 shows the model.

![The Exception Register in the Monitoring Model.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-02-exception-register.svg){#fig-16-02 fig-alt="A model diagram. Three flagged tables, JournalEntry, PurchaseOrder, and PayrollRegister, each feed an exception query through Unpivot and a filter on the flag value; the three exception queries are appended into one Exceptions table. Exceptions relates to Tests on TestID, to Date on EventDate, and to Employee on EmployeeID. The three flagged tables remain in the model as populations, related to Date, and JournalLines relates to JournalEntry."}

## The Monitoring Page

A monitoring page answers three questions in order: which tests are failing, when, and on which documents. A matrix with the tests as rows and the months as columns, each cell holding the number of exceptions, answers the first two at a glance. Shading the cells by rule, darker for more exceptions, turns the matrix into a heat map, in which a row of dark cells and a column of dark cells mean different things. The number stays in each cell, so the shading never carries the meaning alone, the rule Chapter 13 set for every visual. How well a reviewer reads such a display depends on the visual chosen as well as on the reviewer: in a study by Baaske et al. (2025), participants who chose better visualizations identified anomalies more accurately.

Charles River's register shows both patterns. Most of the journal entry, purchase order, and payroll exceptions fall in January, in each of the three years. A cluster in the same month of every year points to how the controls operate at that time of year, when the first entries, orders, and payrolls of a new year are processed, and it tells the auditor where to look and when. One test behaves differently: registers approved by the employee they pay appear in every month, because one employee approves every register, including the approver's own. An exception that recurs in every period is not a lapse to be explained one document at a time. It points to the design of the control, which gives no one the task of approving the approver's pay. The concentration of approval that Chapter 12 found reappears when the exceptions are counted by approver.

The rate puts each count beside its population. Journal entries are few, so even a handful of exceptions is a high rate, while purchase orders run to many thousands and their exceptions are a small fraction. Rates per thousand documents let a reviewer see whether a process is getting better or worse as its volume changes, which a count alone hides.

From the matrix, a drill-through page lists the documents behind any test, so a reviewer can move from a dark cell to the exceptions in it, as Chapter 8 promised. Each exception then needs a disposition, Chapter 8's term for the auditor's conclusion about it: expected, with the evidence that explains it; follow up, with the question to ask; or a misstatement or control deficiency to report. A monitoring report that is run every month accumulates dispositions as well as exceptions, and an exception already explained last month should not cost a reviewer the same time again.

## Row-Level Security

Row-level security restricts the rows of a semantic model that each user can see. Its rules are written in DAX and grouped into roles: each rule belongs to one table and returns true or false for each row, and only the rows for which it returns true are visible to the members of the role (Microsoft, 2026f). A rule filters its table the way a slicer would, and the filter flows through active relationships to the tables on the many side, so a rule on a dimension such as CostCenter also filters the ledger and the budget lines related to it. Microsoft's guidance is to write rules on dimension tables rather than fact tables, for that reason and for speed (Microsoft, 2024). A table that no relationship connects to the filtered dimension is not filtered at all, a fact that matters for any page built on such a table.

A static role filters on a fixed value, such as a role named Sales whose rule keeps the cost center named Sales. A report for ten cost centers would need ten such roles, each to be kept up to date. A dynamic role filters on the identity of the person viewing the report. The DAX function USERPRINCIPALNAME returns the name the user signed in with, their user principal name, which usually looks like an email address. A rule can compare it with a security table that lists, for each user, the cost centers they may see, so that one role serves every manager and access is changed by editing the table, not the role. Roles are additive: a user in two roles sees the rows of both. A user in no role sees no data at all once the report is published with roles, and the rules apply only to people who view the report. The workspace roles Admin, Member, and Contributor can edit the model, so row-level security does not apply to them (Microsoft, 2026f).

Row-level security secures rows. It cannot hide a table, a column, or a measure, and it cannot hide a page. A column of pay rates, for example, is hidden from a role with object-level security, which is defined in the model's TMDL and makes the column invisible to that role, as if it did not exist (Microsoft, 2026c). No setting hides a report page from one role and shows it to another. A page whose totals assume every row, such as an income statement, simply shows the rows the viewer is allowed to see, and nothing on it says the numbers are partial. @tbl-16-03 sets out what each layer of protection covers.

| Layer | Protects | Defined in |
|------------|---------------------------|------------------|
| Row-level security | Rows of the model's tables, by role | Power BI Desktop, Manage roles |
| Object-level security | Tables and columns, by role | The model's TMDL |
| Workspace roles | Who can view, edit, publish, and share | The Power BI service |
| App audiences | Which items of an app each group sees | The Power BI service |
| Sensitivity labels | How content is classified, and protection that travels with exports | Microsoft Purview, applied in Desktop or the service |

: The layers that protect a Power BI report {#tbl-16-03}

A security table is also a list of people with access, and access needs the same control as any other authorization. Kobelsky (2014) counts granting access, and authorizing that grant, among the duties that must be segregated in a computer-supported process: the person who maintains the table should not be the only one who approves its entries. Least privilege, the principle that each user gets only the access the job requires, argues for a design in which a person missing from the table sees nothing, rather than everything. And the table must be reviewed. An access review compares the people who have access with the people who should have it, and its usual findings are accounts of people who have left and people whose job has changed.

Charles River's master data shows why. The CostCenter table records a manager for each cost center, and a role built on that column would look like the natural design. But three of the ten managers of record were terminated in 2024, and none of the three was a manager: their job titles were account executive, sales representative, and inventory specialist. The managers who now run two of those departments are not recorded at all, and another department's manager of record is an analyst. A rule built on the master data would give access to the accounts of people who left and none to the managers who need it. A security table maintained by the controller, approved by someone else, and reviewed periodically avoids both errors. @fig-16-07 shows which tables the rules of Tutorial 16.3 reach.

![What the Security Rules Reach.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-07-rls-reach.svg){#fig-16-07 fig-alt="A model diagram of Charles River Reports with row-level security. A rule on CostCenter filters GLEntry and BudgetLine; a rule on Employee filters LaborTimeEntry; a rule on Item filters SalesInvoiceLine and ProductionCompletionLine for users missing from the Security table. Security sits apart, unrelated, read by the rules. Labels mark which report pages each filtered table feeds, and note that pages such as the Income Statement show only the visible rows without saying so."}


## Publishing and Sharing

A report built in Power BI Desktop reaches its readers through the Power BI service. Choosing **Home > Publish** and a workspace publishes two items, the report and the semantic model it uses, and publishing again replaces the model in the service (Microsoft, 2025c). What a person can do there depends on their license, as @tbl-16-04 summarizes. A free license lets a person publish to their own My workspace and use what they create there, but not share it. Sharing and collaborating need a Pro or Premium Per User license, for the person who shares and, unless the workspace is on a capacity, for the people who view (Microsoft, 2026e). Whether you have such a license depends on your institution, which is why the publishing step of Tutorial 16.3 is optional.

| License | What it allows |
|------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Free | Publish to My workspace and use the content you create, without sharing it |
| Pro | Publish to shared workspaces and share with other Pro users |
| Premium Per User | The Pro capabilities and most Premium features, shared with other Premium Per User users |
| Capacity (Fabric F64 or higher, or Premium) | Pro and Premium Per User users share content with free users, who can view it |

: What each license allows in the Power BI service {#tbl-16-04}

A workspace is a shared container in the service where a team keeps its reports and semantic models, with four roles: Admin, Member, and Contributor can create and edit content, and Viewer can only view and interact with it (Microsoft, 2025f). Department managers should therefore be Viewers, or readers of an app, never members who could edit the model, because row-level security does not apply to editors. An app packages the content of a workspace for its readers, with up to 25 audiences, each of which sees the items chosen for it (Microsoft, 2025b). Audiences show and hide whole items, such as reports, not pages within a report. A page that should not reach managers, such as the Income Statement, belongs in a separate report, built on the same semantic model and shown only to the controller's audience.

A published model holds a copy of the data, which must be refreshed in the service. CharlesRiver.xlsx sits on a local drive, an on-premises source, so a scheduled refresh in the service needs an on-premises data gateway, software installed on a computer that can reach the file and passes the refreshed data to the service. A workbook stored in OneDrive for work or school or in SharePoint can be refreshed without one (Microsoft, 2025e). Either way, the refresh history and its failure notifications are a control: a monitoring report that silently stopped refreshing in March still shows March's exceptions in June, which is why the About page states when the data was last refreshed.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Publish to web creates a link that anyone on the internet can open, with no sign-in. Anyone with the link can reach all the data in the model, including rows that no visual displays, and the option does not work with row-level security at all (Microsoft, 2025d). It is meant for public data, never for financial reports, monitoring results, or anything else confidential. An administrator can turn it off for the whole organization, and an auditor reviewing a Power BI environment should check that this has been done.
:::

Two further controls travel with the content. A sensitivity label from Microsoft Purview, applied with **Sensitivity** on the Home tab of Desktop, classifies a report as, for example, confidential. Applying labels requires a Pro or Premium Per User license and an organization that has enabled them (Microsoft, 2025a). In the service a label does not change who can open the report, which permissions alone decide, but when a reader exports the data to Excel, PowerPoint, or PDF, the label and its protection go with the file, though not with an export to .csv (Microsoft, 2025g). The report's own settings, under **File > Options and settings > Options > Report settings**, decide whether readers may export summarized data, the underlying data, or nothing, and row-level security still limits what they export to the rows they may see (Microsoft, 2026b). @tbl-16-05 compares the ways of sharing a report and what each risks, and @fig-16-08 shows how the pieces fit together.

| Way to share | Reaches | Main risk |
|------------|------------------|---------------------------|
| The .pbix file | Anyone who gets a copy | No row-level security: whoever opens the file in Desktop sees every row |
| A workspace role | Named people or groups | Admins, Members, and Contributors bypass row-level security |
| An app with audiences | Named people or groups, as readers | Hidden items remain reachable by a direct link if hidden content is allowed |
| A share link | People the link names, or the organization | Links spread beyond the readers intended |
| Publish to web | Anyone on the internet | All the model's data becomes public |

: Ways to share a Power BI report and their risks {#tbl-16-05}

![From Desktop to the Report's Readers.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-08-sharing-paths.svg){#fig-16-08 fig-alt="A flow diagram. Power BI Desktop publishes a report and its semantic model to a workspace in the Power BI service, where Admins, Members, and Contributors edit and Viewers read, with row-level security applying only to Viewers. An app built from the workspace gives each audience its own reports. A gateway or OneDrive refreshes the model from the source workbook. A separate path, labeled Publish to web and marked as public and to be avoided for financial data, leads from the workspace to anyone on the internet. A note says that sharing the .pbix file itself bypasses all of these controls."}

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
A report that managers act on every month is a system, and changes to it deserve the change controls that auditors expect of any system. Saving the report as a Power BI project, a .pbip file, stores the model and the report as folders of text files, which version-control tools such as Git can keep and compare, so that every change to a measure or a role can be reviewed before it is published (Microsoft, 2026d). Sensitivity labels are not supported in projects, so a team that needs both keeps its labeled .pbix for publishing. Row-level security also has a cost in speed, because every query carries the role's filters, and Microsoft suggests measuring it with Performance analyzer, on the Optimize tab, with and without View as (Microsoft, 2024).
:::

## Looking Ahead

This chapter has turned the tests of Chapters 8 and 12 into monitoring. You built an exception register that runs the rule tests of three processes with every refresh, set each count beside its population, and found two patterns that call for different responses: exceptions that cluster in the first month of every year, and one that recurs every month because a control has no one to perform it. You reviewed the security of the controller's package and found that the obvious source of its access rules, the managers of record, names people who have left and omits the managers who need access. You built and tested a dynamic role that reads a maintained table and denies access to anyone missing from it, and found the pages that a role leaves silently partial. And you set out how the package and the monitoring report should be published, refreshed, and shared. Most of this work was descriptive and diagnostic analytics, in the terms of @tbl-01-01, and its recommendations, on controls, access, and sharing, are prescriptive.

This chapter completes Part IV. Across its four chapters you have built a model from the Charles River workbook, measured it with DAX, turned it into a reporting package for its managers, and secured and monitored it for its auditors. Part IV closes with a comprehensive case, and Part V then turns to integrated and applied topics that draw on every tool of the book.
